newsitem.title: GERMANY: German job scheme cuts blocked by opposition.
newsitem.headline: German job scheme cuts blocked by opposition.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Friday blocked a labour reform bill that the government was counting on to help it qualify for European monetary union.

The SPD, which controls the Bundesrat upper house, called for parliament's mediation committee to rewrite a package of cuts in training and job creation programmes, saying Bonn's proposal was too harsh.
Cuts in jobs schemes are part of 11 billion marks in savings measures which Finance Minister Theo Waigel urgently wants but which are stalled in parliament due to SPD opposition.
On Thursday, Waigel warned that the SPD's blocking of reforms endangered Germany's ability to meet its projected 1997 budget deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP -- just under the EMU limit of 3.0 percent.
SPD members in the Bundesrat criticised Bonn's proposed cuts at a time when unemployment stands at a postwar record of 4.7 million.
If the mediation group fails to reach a resolution, Bonn still might be able to push the bill into law through its majority in the Bundestag.

Members of the centre-right coalition maintained the measures would need only approval in the Bundestag lower house if an impasse remained in the Bundesrat, but it was unclear if constitutional courts would agree.

Coalition and SPD leaders managed, however, to make progress on a compromise to reduce payments to foreigners seeking asylum in Germany. Officials from both sides said that a deal could be reached by the middle of next week.
German newspaper reports said on Friday that the savings in payments to asylum-seekers could total 400 million mark a year.
